references.text: God gives humans seed-bearing plants and fruit trees for food – the same categories created in verse 11.
It is noted that no shrubs or plants had sprouted yet, providing context to God's command that the earth should bring forth plants in 1:11.
God causes all kinds of trees to grow from the ground, trees that are pleasing to look at and good for food – a continuation of the creation of plant life.
The psalm praises God who makes grass grow for the animals and plants for humans, reflecting the creation of plant life in 1:11.
Just as the earth brings forth its sprouts and a garden causes its seeds to sprout, it reflects the creation principle that the earth should let plants sprout.
The earth drinking rain and bearing useful crops reflects the creation principle that the earth brings forth plants by God's word.
The earth bears fruit on its own – first stalks, then heads of grain, then fully ripe grain – reflecting God's creative order from 1:11.
Complementary days of creation showing the structured progression from vegetation to animals, both under the principle 'each according to its kind'.
Parallel in blessing and the imparting of life: plants (1:11) and animals (1:22) are both given the task to multiply.
Completes the logic of creation: 1:30 shows that animals also receive green plants (created in 1:11) for food.
Prophetic restoration of the created order: God's salvation restores the earth to bear fruit as in 1:11.
A prophetic image of God's blessing: The earth bears fruit as in creation, as a sign of peace.
The covenant law is built on the created order: God's promise of harvest presupposes that the earth can bear fruit (1:11).
Theological contrast: 9:3 changes the food arrangement from the original vegetarian plan in 1:11/29.
Prophetic restoration: The wilderness becomes a fertile field, as a restoration of 1:11.
Prophetic restoration: God's plan to 'plant' and restore the order of creation from Genesis 1:11.
